title: Kangana Ranaut Plays the Nurse Who Stared Down Kasab. Bharat Bhhagya Viddhaata Opens Today.
excerpt: A ₹60 crore thriller about the Cama Hospital staff who saved 400 lives on 26/11 — and the woman who identified the gunman in court.
body:
There is a moment, roughly forty minutes into **Bharat Bhhagya Viddhaata**, when the lights go out. The nurses have just made the call: kill every switch in the building so the gunmen outside might mistake Cama Hospital for an abandoned shell. In the darkness, you can hear breathing — dozens of patients, two women in active labour, and a skeleton staff of nurses who chose to stay.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=8n7bXkykd60</youtube>

This is the story that **Kangana Ranaut** has staked her return on. Not a war epic. Not a political biopic. A hospital. A night shift. A woman named Gita Madhav Gandhare who walked into work on November 26, 2008, expecting nothing more dramatic than the usual ward rounds.

The real Gita is inspired by **Anjali Kulthe**, the nurse at Mumbai's Cama and Albless Hospital who helped evacuate 20 pregnant women while Ajmal Kasab and Abu Ismail moved through the corridors with automatic weapons. Kulthe would later identify Kasab in court — a moment that became pivotal to the prosecution. Director **Manoj Tapadia** builds his entire film around this lesser-known chapter of 26/11, and the result is a contained thriller that trades spectacle for claustrophobia.

The cast is overwhelmingly female, and that's entirely the point. **Girija Oak** plays Sheetal, **Smita Tambe** is Trupti, **Rasika Agashe** is Mohini — names you won't recognise from tabloid headlines but characters drawn from the real women who held the hospital together. **Suhita Thatte** as the matron and **Asha Shelar** as the medical superintendent round out a group that feels lived-in and unglamorous in exactly the right way. Kangana, stripped of the larger-than-life swagger she brought to *Manikarnika* and *Thalaivii*, plays Gita as a woman operating on adrenaline and instinct, and it's arguably her most disciplined performance in years.

Tapadia's screenplay, co-written with **Ritesh Shah** (*Pink*, *Kahaani*), takes its time establishing the hospital geography — which floor, which ward, which staircase. The first half builds methodically, introducing the staff and their routines before the gunshots shatter the calm. When they come, the tension is genuine: two expectant mothers going into labour while terrorists hunt for targets one floor above is the kind of scene that doesn't need a background score to land.

> "When I called to invite her for this screening, she immediately said yes, and I will always be indebted to her." — Kangana Ranaut on Delhi CM Rekha Gupta, who declared the film tax-free

The film isn't without problems. The second half loses spatial clarity — audiences may struggle to track which nurse is hiding where — and the terrorist track wraps up faster than expected, deflating some of the tension that Tapadia painstakingly built. Bollywood Hungama noted that the Marathi-heavy dialogue, while authentic, "would restrict the film's audience outside Maharashtra." And inevitably, comparisons to **Mumbai Diaries 26/11**, the web series that covered similar ground with more scope, will follow the film into theatres.

But what sets this apart is the politics of attention. We've had a dozen 26/11 narratives by now — about the NSG commandos, the Taj Hotel siege, the fishermen who spotted the boats. Cama Hospital has been a footnote. The nurses have been a footnote. A film that centres their courage, even imperfectly, is doing something the industry rarely does: telling a story that matters to people who don't usually get movies made about them.

The music from **G.V. Prakash Kumar** is restrained, with **Sanchit and Ankit Balhara**'s background score doing the heavier lifting. **Ayan Sil**'s cinematography earns its keep with a spiralling open-well staircase shot in the second half that's the film's single most inventive image.

**For NRIs**, this is personal terrain. The 26/11 attacks were the event that froze every Indian abroad in front of a television. If you remember that night — the scrolling tickers, the phone calls that wouldn't connect, the hours of not knowing — this film isn't selling you spectacle. It's reminding you of the people you never heard about. In theatres now.
